name: Battle of Trafalgar
info: A British fleet under Vice-Admiral Nelson defeated a combined French and Spanish fleet under Villeneuve off Cape Trafalgar in 1805, losing no ship, though Nelson was killed; Britain's command of the sea was not tested for over a century.

facts.place: In the Atlantic off Cape Trafalgar, on the south-western coast of Spain
facts.sides: Britain under Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson, 1st Viscount Nelson, with 27 ships of the line, 2,148 cannons and 17,000 crewmen and marines; the French and Spanish navies under Vice-admiral Pierre-Charles Villeneuve, with 33 ships of the line and some 30,000 men, with 2,632 cannons in one count and 2,568 guns in another
facts.outcome: The British took 20 ships of the Franco-Spanish fleet and lost none, though Nelson was killed. Only eleven allied ships escaped to Cádiz, and a storm after the battle wrecked many of the prizes.

t: Nelson sailed his fleet at the Franco-Spanish line in two columns, hoping to break it into pieces and force a chaotic mêlée in which his better-trained crews would prevail.
The British lost no ship; Nelson himself was shot by a French marksman and died about three hours later, shortly before the battle ended.

Napoleon had already given up the invasion of Britain before the battle, and Trafalgar had a limited effect on the War of the Third Coalition, but Britain's command of the sea was not tested for over a century.
dyk: The British ships were painted in a yellow and black pattern, later known as the Nelson Chequer, so that they would be easy to tell from their opponents.
ev: Napoleon plans to take control of the English Channel for an invasion of Britain, and Villeneuve evades Nelson and crosses the Atlantic
Calder fights Villeneuve inconclusively at Cape Finisterre, and two Spanish ships are captured
Villeneuve sails south to Cádiz instead of north to Brest, and the invasion force at Boulogne marches into Germany
Nelson takes command of the British fleet off Cádiz
Villeneuve orders the Combined Fleet to sail from Cádiz
Nelson's two columns break the Franco-Spanish line off Cape Trafalgar, and Nelson is mortally wounded
Commodore Cosmao leads a sortie from Cádiz and a storm wrecks many of the prizes
Strachan's squadron captures the four ships that had fled under Dumanoir

sections.background:
In 1805 the First French Empire under Napoleon Bonaparte was the dominant military land power on the European continent, while the Royal Navy prevailed at sea through disruptive blockades. When the Third Coalition declared war on France after the short-lived Peace of Amiens, Napoleon renewed his determination to invade Britain. To bring his invasion flotilla to England he needed to wrest control of the English Channel from the Royal Navy. His plan was for the French and Spanish fleets in the Mediterranean and at Cádiz to break through the blockade and join forces in the Caribbean, then return, help the fleet at Brest to emerge, and together clear the Channel.

Early in 1805 Nelson blockaded Toulon loosely, hoping to lure the French out. Villeneuve evaded him when storms blew the British off station, passed the Strait of Gibraltar, joined the Spanish fleet at Cádiz and sailed for the Caribbean. Nelson pursued and missed him by just days in the West Indies as a result of false information. Villeneuve returned to Europe, and Calder fought him inconclusively at Cape Finisterre on 22 July. Ordered to Brest, Villeneuve instead sailed south to Cádiz on 11 August. On 25 August the invasion force near Boulogne broke camp and marched into Germany, which ended the immediate threat of invasion.

Nelson, who had returned home, sailed in HMS Victory on 15 September and took command off Cádiz on 28 September. On 16 September Napoleon ordered the ships at Cádiz to put to sea, land soldiers at Naples and fight if they met a numerically inferior British fleet.
sections.forces:
On 21 October Nelson had 27 ships of the line with 2,148 cannons and a total of 17,000 crewmen and marines. His flagship Victory, captained by Thomas Masterman Hardy, was one of three 100-gun first-rates; he also had four 98-gun second-rates and 20 third-rates, three of them 64-gun ships then being phased out. There were also four frigates, a schooner and a cutter. The second in command, Vice-Admiral Cuthbert Collingwood, led one column in the 100-gun Royal Sovereign.

Villeneuve, flying his flag in Bucentaure, had 33 ships of the line, among them some of the largest in the world: the Spanish Santísima Trinidad of 130 guns and the 112-gun Príncipe de Asturias and Santa Ana. The Spanish contributed 15 ships of the line and the French 18, with some 30,000 men and 2,632 cannons; another count gives nearly 30,000 men and 2,568 guns. The fleet also had five frigates and two brigs, all French. Its crews included few experienced sailors, ships had been kept in harbour for years by the blockade, and gunnery was neglected. Villeneuve's ships were also more than two thousand men short of the force needed to sail.

Nelson meant to cut the opposing line in three, approaching in two columns at nearly a right angle, one towards the centre and one towards the rear, and to force a mêlée. He told his captains that no captain could do very wrong who placed his ship alongside an enemy's. Villeneuve guessed that Nelson would drive at his line, but, fearing that his inexperienced officers could not keep formation in more than one group, kept a single line.
sections.course:
On 21 October the Franco-Spanish fleet formed a sprawling, uneven line. At 8 a.m. Villeneuve ordered it to turn about and return to Cádiz, and in the light, shifting wind this took nearly an hour and a half, leaving an uneven crescent drawn out nearly 5 miles (8 km) long. At 11:45 Nelson signalled "England expects that every man will do his duty". Nelson in Victory led the northern column and Collingwood in Royal Sovereign the leeward one. As the wind was very light, the leading British ships were under heavy fire from several allied ships for almost an hour before their own guns could bear.

At noon Villeneuve signalled "engage the enemy" and Fougueux fired her first shot at Royal Sovereign, which, her bottom recently cleaned, outran the rest and broke the line just astern of Santa Ana with a double-shotted raking broadside. At 12:45 Victory cut the line between Bucentaure and Redoutable and fired a treble-shotted raking broadside through Bucentaure's stern, which killed and wounded some 200 to 400 of its 800 men and dismasted it. Victory then locked masts with Redoutable, and a musket bullet fired from Redoutable's mizzentop struck Nelson in the left shoulder and passed through his spine.

Temeraire fired a carronade on Redoutable's exposed crew; at 13:55 Captain Lucas, with 99 fit men out of 643, surrendered. Santísima Trinidad surrendered after three hours. The allied centre and rear were gradually overwhelmed. Gravina was wounded, and Churruca and Alcalá-Galiano were killed after ordering their ships not to surrender. Nelson died at half-past four, three hours after being hit.
sections.aftermath:
The British took 20 vessels of the Franco-Spanish fleet and lost none. Redoutable sank, Santísima Trinidad and Argonauta were scuttled by the British, Achille exploded, Intrépide and San Agustín burned, and Aigle, Berwick, Fougueux and Monarca were wrecked in the gale that followed. Dumanoir led four ships away from the fighting; they were captured by Strachan's squadron on 4 November at the Battle of Cape Ortegal. Only eleven allied ships escaped to Cádiz and only five were seaworthy. Gravina passed command to Commodore Cosmao on 23 October and died months later of his wounds.

Cosmao sailed out with ships and frigates to try to recapture prizes, and French frigates retook two Spanish ships, Santa Ana and Neptuno, whose crews rose against their British prize crews. In the heavy seas Collingwood ordered his ships to cast off their prizes, and the allied squadron lost one French and two Spanish vessels. Indomptable was wrecked with 1,200 men on board, of whom no more than 100 were saved. The British burnt or sank four more prizes, and only four reached Britain. On 27 October he offered to set Spanish wounded ashore, and the Spanish governor and Gravina released British prisoners in exchange.

Villeneuve was captured with his flagship and taken to Britain. After his parole in 1806 he was found dead in an inn on the road to Paris with six stab wounds, officially recorded as suicide. Nelson's body, kept in a barrel of brandy, went home for a state funeral. Napoleon kept the defeat secret for over a month.
sections.sources:
The battle is known through those who were there. The signal made at 11:45 comes from Lieutenant Pasco, who recalled that Nelson first wished to say "England confides" and agreed to "expects" because that word was in the signal vocabulary. Surgeon William Beatty heard Nelson murmur "Thank God I have done my duty", while his chaplain, Alexander Scott, recorded the last words as "God and my country". The Nelson historian Craig Cabell has suggested that Nelson was reciting his own prayer, in which the words "God" and "my country" are closely linked. Collingwood's letter to the Admiralty of November 1805 describes the storm.

Accounts of the allied sortie differ. Cosmao claimed in his report that the rescue plan was entirely his idea, but Vice-Admiral Escaño recorded a meeting of Spanish and French commodores at which it was discussed and agreed. Counts of the allied guns differ, 2,632 or 2,568, and the allied ships lost are counted as 18 captured or destroyed, or as 20 taken.

The news was controlled in France. Napoleon did not hear of the battle for weeks and kept the defeat a closely guarded secret for over a month, and a fabricated text declaring a spectacular victory for the French and Spanish was published and attributed to Le Moniteur Universel. Historians also differ on why the losses were so uneven. Some attribute the disparity less to Nelson's tactics than to the fighting readiness of the fleets, though Villeneuve's fleet had just spent months at sea, which supports the view that the leaders' morale was the main difference.
sections.legacy:
The victory confirmed Britain's naval supremacy in the Napoleonic Wars. Napoleon had already abandoned his invasion plans before the battle and never revived them, and the Royal Navy was never again seriously challenged by the French fleet in a large-scale engagement. The battle did not end the French naval challenge: Britain acted at Copenhagen in 1807 and elsewhere in 1808 to stop smaller navies falling into French hands, and Napoleon's shipbuilding programme had produced a fleet of 80 ships of the line by 1814. For almost ten years the Royal Navy maintained a close blockade of French bases. Trafalgar had a negligible impact on the rest of the War of the Third Coalition: less than two months later Napoleon defeated the Coalition at Austerlitz, and the Napoleonic Wars continued for another ten years.

The Royal Navy's dominance was not meaningfully tested until Jutland in the First World War. Modern analyses suggest that relative economic strength was an important underlying cause of British naval mastery, though Trafalgar was given as the reason at the time. Nelson's unorthodox tactics were seldom emulated by later generations.

Nelson remains Britain's greatest naval war hero. Monuments to him include the one on Glasgow Green of 1806, Nelson's Pillar in Dublin, erected in 1808 and destroyed by a bombing in 1966, Nelson's Monument in Edinburgh, and Nelson's Column in Montreal. London's Trafalgar Square is named for the battle, and Nelson's Column there was finished in 1843. In 2005 a Fleet Review in the Solent had 167 ships from 35 nations.

summary: At Trafalgar on 21 October 1805 Nelson's fleet broke the line of a larger Franco-Spanish fleet under Villeneuve and took 20 ships without losing one, though Nelson was killed. It ended any real French effort to invade Britain and left the Royal Navy's command of the sea untested for over a century.

notes: Disputed or inconsistent in the text: the lead says 18 ships were captured or destroyed, the narrative says the British took 20; guns are 2632 in the Fleets section and 2568 in the Prelude; I gave both.
No casualty totals for either side are given, so the aftermath gives only the ship-level figures the text has.

The text has no real section on sources; the sources section is built from the quoted witnesses and the disagreements the text itself reports (Pasco, Beatty, Scott, Cabell, Cosmao v Escaño, Napoleon's censorship). Editor should read it first.
Legacy: left out the Trafalgar Way and the 1905 gala details for length; 'Nelson remains Britain's greatest naval war hero' is the text's own wording.
The text calls Nelson's plan 'brilliant' and the result 'decisive'; I avoided both words. The dyk Nelson Chequer is as given.
The Villeneuve death account: the text says six stab wounds from a dining knife, officially suicide; the text does not itself dispute it.
